2027-06-19.title: Fifth Saturday of the Apostles · Sts Gervasius and Protasius
2027-06-19.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: The law is holy, but sin seized its opportunity
2027-06-19.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations and founded the Churches. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and since Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed in place of the Queen of Heaven. Sts Gervasius and Protasius, martyrs of Milan, are listed in the First Set calendar for today without proper readings; the readings are those of the day. In the Latin calendar today is the optional memorial of St Romuald, abbot.
2027-06-19.verse: Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the treasury.
theo: Saint Paul is never more honest than in the seventh chapter of his letter to the Romans. He has just said that Christians have died to the law through the body of Christ, and he knows the objection that will come at once: is the law then something bad? “What then should we say? That the law is sin? By no means!” The law is not the enemy. It is a lamp that shows what is in the room. “If it had not been for the law, I would not have known sin. I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, ‘You shall not covet.’” Paul chooses the last of the Ten Commandments, the only one that concerns the heart rather than the hand. No court can see covetousness; only God and conscience can. And here Paul describes something every one of us has felt: “sin, seizing an opportunity in the commandment, produced in me all kinds of covetousness.” Tell a child not to open a box, and the box becomes the most interesting thing in the house. Sin is a parasite. It has no life of its own; it lives on what is good and twists it. The same commandment that “promised life proved to be death to me,” not because the commandment was bad, but because “sin, seizing an opportunity in the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me.” The word “deceived” takes us back to the garden, where the serpent used God's own command to plant suspicion in Eve's heart. Paul's verdict stands firm: “So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good.” What is wrong is not the law but the heart that cannot keep it.

Why does this matter in the Season of the Apostles? Because the law can show us the right road but cannot give us legs to walk on it. In later Jewish tradition the feast of Weeks, Pentecost, came to be remembered as the day the Law was given at Sinai. Fifty days after the Resurrection, God gave his people something the tablets of stone could not give: the Holy Spirit, writing the law of love on human hearts, as Jeremiah and Ezekiel had promised. St Augustine summed it up in a famous sentence (in substance): the law was given so that grace might be sought; grace was given so that the law might be fulfilled. The apostles went out after Pentecost not with a longer list of rules but with the power to keep the commandments from within. The tenth commandment still stands, and it is still hard: in a world of advertisements, comparison and endless scrolling, covetousness is the air we breathe. But the Spirit who came at Pentecost is stronger than the desire that grows in the dark. Paul will cry out a few verses later, “Who will rescue me from this body of death?” and answer at once, “Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord!” (Romans 7:24–25).

The Gospel puts a living picture beside Paul's teaching. Jesus is in the Temple in the last days before his Passion. He warns against the scribes “who like to walk around in long robes, and to be greeted with respect in the marketplaces, and to have the best seats in the synagogues and places of honor at banquets!” We must read this carefully. Jesus is not condemning all scribes; only a few verses earlier he told a scribe who answered wisely, “You are not far from the kingdom of God” (Mark 12:34). He is warning against a temptation that lives in every religious person in every age, in priests and lay leaders, in parish committees and prayer groups: the love of being seen. Then Jesus sits down “opposite the treasury, and watched the crowd putting money into the treasury.” He watches. The rich put in large sums, and no doubt the sound of their coins was loud. “A poor widow came and put in two small copper coins, which are worth a penny.” Jesus calls his disciples, as if to give them a lesson for their whole apostolic life: “Truly I tell you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the treasury. For all of them have contributed out of their abundance; but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on.” The covetous heart of Romans 7 grasps; the widow's heart lets go. She is the opposite of the scribes who “devour widows’ houses”: they take, she gives. And she gives not out of what is left over, but out of her whole life. Within a few days the Lord who watched her will give everything he has, his own body and blood, for the life of the world. The widow is the last person Jesus praises in Mark's account of his public ministry, and she is a picture of him.

Today the First Set calendar also lists Sts Gervasius and Protasius, martyrs of the early Church in Milan. Little is known of their lives. In 386, during a hard struggle between St Ambrose and the imperial court, the bishop found their bodies and laid them beneath the altar of his new basilica in Milan, saying (in substance) that the victorious victims should rest in the place where Christ is the victim. St Augustine, who was in Milan at the time and not yet baptised, recalls in his Confessions the joy of the people and the healing of a blind man. Every altar stone with relics, and every Holy Qurbana offered over the bones of the saints, recalls that day: the martyrs, like the widow, gave everything, and their offering is joined to the one sacrifice of Christ.
outline: Two pictures: a commandment that shows sin, and a widow who gives everything.
The tenth commandment and the heart that covets.
Point 2 · Grace to fulfil the law
Pentecost writes the law on the heart.

The love of being seen, and the love that gives its whole life.
“She out of her poverty has put in everything she had.”
live: Name one thing you have been wanting because someone else has it. Give thanks today for three things you already have.
All she had to live on (Mark 12:44)
Give something this week that you will actually miss: time, money or comfort, quietly and without being seen.
fathers: The law was given so that grace might be sought; grace was given so that the law might be fulfilled. It was not the fault of the law that it was not kept, but the fault of the proud mind that trusted itself.

The widow gave two small coins, yet she was preferred to the rich, because God does not look at the amount but at the heart and the means of the giver. Let no one say, I am poor and have nothing to give: she was poorer than you, and she gave all.
magis: According to Christian tradition, the Law is holy, spiritual and good, yet still imperfect: like a tutor it shows what must be done, but does not of itself give the strength, the grace of the Spirit, to fulfil it.
Jesus enjoins his disciples to prefer him to everything and everyone; the example of the poor widow of Jerusalem, who gave out of her poverty all that she had to live on, is put before them.
The tenth commandment forbids greed and the desire to amass earthly goods without limit; the sensitive appetite leads us to desire what we do not have, and disordered desire must be governed.
saints: Sts Gervasius and Protasius, early martyrs of Milan, whose relics St Ambrose discovered in 386 and placed beneath the altar of his basilica (listed in the First Set calendar without proper readings). Latin calendar: St Romuald (about 952–1027), abbot, founder of the Camaldolese monks, who joined the hermit's life with the common life of monks.

19–24 June: the end of the fifth week and the sixth week of the Season of the Apostles. Sat 19: Sts Gervasius and Protasius, martyrs, are listed in the First Set calendar without proper readings; in the Latin calendar, St Romuald. Sun 20: Sixth Sunday of the Apostles. Mon 21: St Aloysius Gonzaga is listed without proper readings (in the Latin calendar an obligatory memorial). Tue 22: Sts John Fisher and Thomas More, martyrs, with proper readings. Thu 24: the Birth of John the Baptist. Then Sun 27: Seventh Sunday of the Apostles, the last Sunday of the season; Tue 29: Sts Peter and Paul, Apostles, an important feast and a day of obligation.
2027-06-19.prayer: Holy Father, your law is holy and just and good, but our hearts are weak and easily deceived. Send us the Holy Spirit whom you poured out at Pentecost, to write your commandments on our hearts and to heal the desire that grasps at what is not ours. Lord Jesus, you watched the poor widow give everything she had, and you gave your whole life for us: teach us to give without being seen and to trust you with all we have. With Sts Gervasius and Protasius and all your martyrs, may we offer ourselves with you on the altar. To the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit be glory for ever. Amen.
altar: The widow put her whole life into the treasury; at the Holy Qurbana Christ places his whole life, his Body and Blood, on the altar for us. When we bring our gifts and ourselves to the altar, he does not count the coins; he looks at the heart and joins our small offering to his great one.

quick: Paul: the law is holy, but sin seized its opportunity in the commandment and deceived me.
Grace is given so that the law may be fulfilled: the Spirit of Pentecost writes the law on our hearts.
Jesus watches the treasury: the poor widow gives more than all the rich, everything she had to live on.
2027-06-19.action: Give something today that you will really miss, quietly and without telling anyone.
2027-06-19.question: Do I give from what is left over, or from my life?

family.explain: Jesus sat in the Temple and watched people put money in the offering box. Rich people put in a lot. Then a poor widow came and put in two tiny coins, all the money she had. Jesus told his friends that she had given more than everyone else, because the rich gave what they did not need, but she gave everything. God does not look at how big our gift is; he looks at how much love is in it.
family.intention: We pray for widows, for poor families, and for everyone who shares even when they have little.
family.ask: Ask: “What small thing can each of us give this week with a big heart?”

illus: In a parish in Kuttanad, during a monsoon when the fields were under water, the vicar announced a collection for families whose houses had been damaged. That Sunday an old widow who lived alone near the canal came to the sacristy after the Qurbana with a small cloth bundle. Inside were a few coins and some folded notes, less than two hundred rupees. ‘Achen, I kept this for my funeral,’ she said, ‘but the children whose houses fell need it now. God will see to my funeral.’ The vicar tried to give it back, and she refused. That evening he told the parish council what had happened, without naming her. By the end of the week the collection was three times larger than anyone had expected. ‘She gave the least,’ one of the members said, ‘and she moved everyone else to give.’

pm.open: Holy Spirit, you came at Pentecost to write the law of love on our hearts. Come now, heal our desires, and make us generous like the widow whom Jesus praised. Amen.
share: I would not have known what it is to covet if the law had not said, “You shall not covet” (Romans 7:7). What do I covet?
So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good (Romans 7:12). Do I see God's commandments as a gift or as a burden?
Beware of the scribes, who like to walk around in long robes (Mark 12:38). Where do I like to be seen and praised?
She out of her poverty has put in everything she had (Mark 12:44). What is God asking me to give?
interc: For the Church in this Season of the Apostles, that her ministers may serve without seeking honour or the best seats.
For widows and for women who live alone, that they may be respected, protected and never exploited.
For those caught in covetousness, envy and debt, that the Spirit may heal their hearts of the desire for more.
For families affected by the monsoon rains and floods, and for all who help them.
For the martyrs of our own time, that their sacrifice may bear fruit in the Church.
pm.close: Father, you see what is given in secret and you rejoice in a generous heart. Write your law in us by your Spirit, and teach us to give our whole lives with your Son, who gave himself for us. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, Saint Paul asks a question today: is the law sin? And he answers, “By no means!” (Romans 7:7). God's commandments are holy and just and good. The problem is not the commandment; the problem is the heart.

Paul gives an example: “You shall not covet.” This is the only commandment about the heart. As soon as we hear it, we notice how much we want what others have: their phone, their house, their success, their life. Sin is like a parasite. It takes the good commandment and twists it against us.

That is why we need more than a law. We need the Holy Spirit. At Pentecost the Spirit came to write the law of love on our hearts. Saint Augustine said: the law was given so that we might look for grace; grace was given so that the law might be kept.

In the Gospel Jesus sits opposite the treasury of the Temple and watches. The rich put in large sums. A poor widow puts in two small coins. And Jesus says that she has given more than all of them, because she gave “everything she had, all she had to live on” (Mark 12:44).

The covetous heart grasps; the widow's heart lets go. She is a picture of Jesus himself, who a few days later gave his whole life on the Cross, and who gives himself to us today in the Holy Qurbana. Let us bring him not what is left over, but our whole life. Amen.
kids: Children, a poor lady put two tiny coins in the offering box at the Temple. Jesus said she gave more than all the rich people, because she gave everything she had, with love. God does not count how much we give; he looks at how much we love. What can you give to Jesus today with a big heart?

The holy law that shows us our sin, the grace of the Spirit that fulfils it, and the widow who gives her whole life.

Sin, the parasite that twists the good.
q: The law of the Lord is perfect, reviving the soul;
So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good.
points.apply: Pray the Ten Commandments slowly tonight as an examination of conscience, pausing at the tenth.

sub: The Spirit of Pentecost writes the law on the heart.
q: If you do well, will you not be accepted? And if you do not do well, sin is lurking at the door; its desire is for you, but you must master it.
Wretched man that I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?

points.h: All she had to live on
sub: The Lord who watches the treasury.
The widow, a picture of Christ.
q: Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the Lord, and will be repaid in full.
For all of them have contributed out of their abundance; but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on.
points.apply: Make one hidden gift this week that costs you something real.

concl: The law is holy, but only the Spirit can make us keep it from the heart.
The widow gave her whole life, as Christ gave his: let us bring our whole lives to the altar.
2027-06-19.resolve: This week, examine your heart with the tenth commandment, call on the Holy Spirit when envy rises, and make one hidden gift that costs you something.
